Offense: During co-host Robin Quiver's news segment, Howard Stern commented on a story about the late-singer Selena who had just recently been murdered.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bXk_gjeEKKQ

During the segment, the crew listens to Selena's music while gunshot sound effects play and Stern commented that the music didn't make him feel anything and that he doesn't understand why she was popular. He said that Spanish people have the worst taste in music.

Controversy: The comedy bit angered Hispanic groups and fans of Selena.

http://selenatrial.selenaforever.com/Selena_Archive/04_06_95.html

Controversial deejay Howard Stern, widely known for his tasteless humor, has really hit a nerve this time. He picked on slain Tejano music superstar Selena and outraged Hispanic communities around the state -- including Houston, where his radio show isn't even aired.

Hundreds of Selena fans called local radio stations Wednesday to vent their anger after hearing about Stern's ridicule and how he played Selena's music -- with the sound of gunfire.

City leaders showed anger at the City Council meeting, and a local state representative publicly condemned Stern's remarks.

Result: Howard Stern apologized in Spanish.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ysSEcIKXiXg

English translation: http://www.nydailynews.com/archives/entertainment/real-shocker-stern-apology-selena-comments-article-1.689006

The statement itself, which he read with a Selena song playing in the background, began, "As you know, I'm a satirical person. My remarks on Selena's tragic death were certainly not made with the aim of causing even more anguish to her family, friends and those who loved her."

A few minutes after he read the statement, he compared it to John Kennedy's famous "Ich bin ein Berliner."

However, the apology was not accepted by the National Hispanic Media Coalition, which called for a boycott.

http://articles.latimes.com/1995-04-11/entertainment/ca-53295_1_howard-stern

The controversy would eventually die down and be forgotten. Today, Howard Stern is a judge on America's Got Talent on NBC.

It depends on what you plan on using it for or what you want out of it. The 10/22 is a more universal gun,being semiautomatic. Where the Savage you are considering is a bolt action. Bolt actions are supposed to be more accurate and reliable in adverse conditions. If you are looking to use it for accuracy shooting, go with the Savage. If you are wanting to use it for hunting, target practice and defense I would go with the Ruger. There is a lot of aftermarket stuff for the10/22. Folding stock's, 30 round magazines etc. By the way, I would never bet my life on a rim fire cartridge. It is not uncommon for the round to not go off. ( Just my opinion ) That is what a 22 is.
The 10/22s I own are not as accurate as I would like. I enjoy my bolt action single shot. I shoot less and I hit my target more. The 10/22 is a good gun though.

I personally like a Marlin 60 over a 10/22. Everyone says go with 10/22 because of all the aftermarket stuff, but you have to ask your self whats important...fashion accessories or something that shoots well. From my experience the 60 is a little bit smoother to operate. It has a little lighter trigger with a shorter pull. It will eat damn near anything you feed it (although the 10/22 isn't bad for that either).

Also if you DO want a semi-auto 22 with lots of after market options, a M&P 15-22 is a darn good 22 and most ar15 accessories will work on it.

>We were in a restaurant and the TV was on,” showing the coming presidential election, Ms. H-C said. “I said I was excited that Obama was going to be re-elected.” The client’s “whole body stiffened, and it was clear he was not an Obama supporter.”

>Even though the contracts were all but signed, he dropped out of sight; ultimately, she received a call from the human resources department telling her the company decided to “go in a different direction.”

>“I lost $30,000 to $40,000,” she said. “The lesson was to be very aware of other people’s beliefs and to be very delicate about what could trigger them.”

I think the lesson is for people who are offended by differences of political opinion to calm down. To be fair, though, you never know if that sort of story is just coincidence.

Here's another lesson. Don't expect all that corporate data mining of your online activities to be used innocently. Losing your opportunity to make money in a perpetually poor economy is probably the most likely bad outcome you'll personally see from all the spying.

I recently started wondering if companies are going to look at the big data gathered about you to find out if there are any reasons the company should not hire you should you apply for a job there.

I also wonder how the public would react to a credit bureau-like database that assigns you a job worthiness or work history score that other companies can purchase. In other words, like companies you do business with report late payments and debt to credit score companies, employers would report terminations and job-related issues. A firing for incompetence could last 7 years before it drops off your record. It would be a beefed-up version of employment verification.

They are already requesting credit scores and a few companies are starting to request Facebook and Twitter passwords.

The need to work for a living could be the greatest threat to personal freedom for most of us. Watch every move or stay off line at the same time that on line activities become more essential to normal life. Then again, you can't stay off line either because then you will be profiled as a 'non-team player' or something worse.

Nobody can or will enforce a time limit. Those data files will just keep growing. Basically, just shut up, work your Facebook to appear as 'normal' as possible, and try not to complain about anything. Employers don't like complainers.

On the other hand, to protect from government, we need to have as many people being vocal as possible -- the very opposite thing that we need to do to protect from business. A conundrum. We have serious problems here.
